name: EMPI Coordinator
description: Learn enterprise master patient index concepts, matching workflows, and identity stewardship.
longDescription: Build practical skills for coordinating patient identity across systems: EMPI fundamentals, deterministic and probabilistic matching, duplicate review, merge decisions, and audit-aware operations.
primaryGoal: Develop coordinator-level judgment for patient identity matching, stewardship, and operational accountability.
disclaimer: Educational content only. Not medical advice, legal advice, or HIPAA compliance guidance. Do not enter real PHI into Ask Expert. Follow your organization's policies and qualified compliance review.

capabilities.title: Learn
capabilities.description: Follow a structured path through EMPI fundamentals and stewardship workflows.

capabilities.title: Ask
capabilities.description: Ask questions grounded in EMPI knowledge topics.

capabilities.title: Scenarios

capabilities.title: Quiz
capabilities.description: Test your understanding of matching concepts and terminology.

systemPrompt: You are the EMPI Coordinator expert inside Guardian. Help users learn enterprise master patient index (EMPI) and master patient index (MPI) operations: patient matching, identity stewardship, duplicate review, merge/unmerge concepts, survivorship, and audit accountability. Use clear, practical language for healthcare data stewards and coordinators. Stay within educational scope. Never provide medical advice, legal advice, or definitive HIPAA compliance guidance. Do not request or process real patient identifiers or PHI. When uncertain, say so and recommend following organizational policy and qualified review.
responseRules: Keep answers focused on EMPI/MPI operations and stewardship workflows.
Use fictional examples only; never ask for real patient data.
Distinguish educational guidance from organization-specific policy.
Reference relevant learning topics when helpful.
Encourage documentation, audit trails, and escalation when match confidence is unclear.
starterQuestions: What is the difference between an MPI and an EMPI?
When should a potential duplicate go to manual review?
What is a golden record in patient identity management?
How do deterministic and probabilistic matching differ?

roadmap.title: EMPI Fundamentals
roadmap.description: Understand why enterprise patient identity exists and who the key stakeholders are.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of EMPI in care delivery and data exchange
Identify common identifiers used in patient matching

roadmap.title: Patient Matching
roadmap.description: Learn how records are linked, scored, and routed for review.
learningObjectives: Know when to auto-link versus escalate to manual review

knowledgeTopics.title: Purpose of EMPI
knowledgeTopics.summary: An Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI) creates a trusted view of patient identity across multiple source systems.
details: Hospitals and health systems often have many applications, each with its own medical record number (MRN).
EMPI links those records to a single enterprise identity so clinicians and analysts see consistent patient context.
Accurate identity supports clinical safety, care coordination, reporting, and revenue cycle integrity.
Poor identity quality creates duplicate records, split records, and downstream operational risk.

examples.title: Cross-facility patient
examples.description: A patient registered in the ED and again in outpatient rehab may appear as two records until EMPI matching links or flags them for review.

keyPoints: EMPI is an operational system of record for identity, not clinical content
Identity quality is a shared responsibility across registration, HIM, and IT
Stewardship workflows exist because perfect automation is impossible
commonMistakes: Treating EMPI as only an IT project instead of a clinical operations program
Assuming one strong identifier eliminates all duplicates
starterQuestions: Why do health systems need an EMPI?
Who owns patient identity quality in a hospital?

knowledgeTopics.title: Patient Identifiers and Match Keys
knowledgeTopics.summary: Matching relies on demographic and identifier fields, each with different reliability and privacy constraints.
details: Common match keys include legal name components, date of birth, sex, address, phone, and government identifiers where permitted.
Facility MRNs are local to a source system and are not portable enterprise identifiers by themselves.
Enterprise identifiers (enterprise ID, universal ID) are assigned after identity resolution.
Organizations define which fields are required at registration because missing data weakens matching.

examples.title: Weak registration data
examples.description: Records with missing DOB or generic names like 'Baby Boy' increase false positives and manual review volume.

keyPoints: Data quality at registration directly affects EMPI performance
Not every identifier should be used in automated matching
Policies govern use of sensitive identifiers
commonMistakes: Using outdated addresses as high-confidence keys
Ignoring nickname and maiden name variants in matching rules
starterQuestions: What makes a good match key?
Why are MRNs insufficient as a universal patient ID?

knowledgeTopics.title: Deterministic vs Probabilistic Matching
knowledgeTopics.summary: Deterministic rules require exact agreement on defined fields; probabilistic models score similarity across weighted attributes.
details: Deterministic matching is fast and explainable, e.g. exact match on enterprise ID or a defined composite key.
Probabilistic matching assigns weights to fields (name, DOB, address) and produces a match score.
High scores may auto-link; borderline scores route to manual review queues.
Algorithms may include phonetic name matching, nickname tables, and address normalization.

examples.title: Nickname variation
examples.description: Robert vs Bob may score highly on DOB and address but require nickname logic rather than exact first-name match.

keyPoints: No single algorithm fits all populations and use cases
Tuning thresholds balances missed duplicates against false merges
Manual review is a feature, not a failure
commonMistakes: Auto-merging on name and DOB alone in high-risk populations
Disabling review queues to reduce backlog without measuring harm
starterQuestions: What does a match score represent?

knowledgeTopics.title: Scores, Thresholds, and Review Queues
knowledgeTopics.summary: Thresholds translate algorithm output into operational actions: auto-link, review, or create new identity.
details: Organizations typically define auto-link, manual review, and reject/create bands.
Review queues should prioritize high-risk pairs and aging worklists.
Metrics include duplicate rate, auto-link rate, review turnaround, and post-merge correction rate.
Threshold changes should be governed, tested, and communicated to stewardship teams.

examples.title: Borderline score
examples.description: Two records share name and DOB but different SSN last-four values; coordinator escalates instead of merging.

keyPoints: Threshold tuning is ongoing operations work
Safety favors caution when identifiers conflict
commonMistakes: Clearing queues by lowering thresholds without quality monitoring
Treating all manual reviews as equal priority
starterQuestions: What happens when a pair falls below the auto-link threshold?

knowledgeTopics.title: Stewardship: Duplicates, Merges, and Overlays
knowledgeTopics.summary: Data stewards adjudicate potential duplicates and decide how source records roll up to an enterprise identity.
details: A duplicate pair is two records believed to represent the same person.
Merge combines identities so downstream systems reference one enterprise ID.
Overlay links source records to a golden record while preserving source attributes where appropriate.
Unmerge reverses an incorrect merge and must be rare, controlled, and heavily audited.
Survivorship rules decide which source value wins for each data element on the golden record.

examples.title: Twin or mother-baby edge case
examples.description: Similar demographics around delivery may create false positives; stewards apply policy and additional verification.

keyPoints: Incorrect merges are high-impact patient safety events
Stewards document rationale for non-obvious decisions
Escalation paths exist for ambiguous cases
commonMistakes: Merging because names look similar without checking conflicting identifiers
Using unmerge as a routine cleanup tool
starterQuestions: What is the difference between merge and overlay?
When should I escalate instead of deciding alone?

knowledgeTopics.title: Audit, Accountability, and Policy
knowledgeTopics.summary: Identity changes must be traceable, policy-aligned, and reviewable for compliance and patient safety.
details: Audit logs should capture who changed identity, when, why, and which records were affected.
Coordinators follow organizational policies for break-glass access and exception handling.
Training and periodic competency review reduce inconsistent stewardship decisions.
Educational content does not replace organizational compliance review or legal counsel.

examples.title: Post-merge correction
examples.description: A merge is reversed after discovery of conflicting insurance identifiers; audit trail supports investigation and notification workflows.

keyPoints: Accountability is as important as algorithm accuracy
Policy defines acceptable evidence for merge decisions
Never enter real PHI into training tools outside approved environments
commonMistakes: Making identity changes without ticket or case documentation
Assuming vendor defaults match local policy without validation
starterQuestions: What should an identity audit log include?
How do coordinators work with compliance teams?

glossary.definition: Enterprise Master Patient Index — a system that resolves and maintains patient identity across an organization.
Master Patient Index — often used interchangeably with EMPI, though some organizations distinguish enterprise vs facility scope.
The authoritative enterprise view of a patient's identity built from contributing source records.
A match based on exact agreement of predefined fields or keys.
A match based on weighted similarity scoring across demographic attributes.
A numeric confidence output used to route pairs to auto-link, review, or reject actions.
Linking source records to an enterprise identity while retaining source-specific attributes.
Rules that determine which source value populates each field on the golden record.

quizzes.title: EMPI Fundamentals Quiz
quizzes.description: Check your understanding of EMPI purpose and identifiers.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an EMPI?
options: Store clinical notes from the EHR
Maintain a trusted enterprise view of patient identity across systems
questions.explanation: EMPI focuses on identity resolution across systems, not clinical document storage.

questions.question: A facility MRN alone is always sufficient as a universal enterprise patient identifier.
questions.explanation: MRNs are typically local to a source system; enterprise identity requires cross-system resolution.

questions.question: Which factor most directly weakens automated patient matching?
questions.explanation: Registration data quality is foundational; missing DOB or weak names increase errors and review volume.

quizzes.title: Stewardship Quiz
quizzes.description: Test merge, overlay, and accountability concepts.

questions.question: Two records share name and DOB but have conflicting government identifier fragments. Best next step?
options: Auto-merge immediately to reduce queue volume
Escalate or manually review per policy before merging
Ignore because name and DOB match
questions.explanation: Conflicting high-risk identifiers require manual review and documented rationale.

questions.question: What is survivorship?
options: Deleting inactive patients from all systems
Rules that decide which source value wins on the golden record
A type of probabilistic match score
questions.explanation: Survivorship governs which contributing source populates each attribute on the enterprise identity.

questions.question: Unmerge should be a routine way to clean up duplicate review backlogs.
questions.explanation: Unmerge is a controlled, exceptional correction for incorrect merges — not routine queue management.

scenarios.title: Borderline Duplicate Pair
scenarios.notice: Fictional training scenario. Do not use real patient information.
scenarios.context: You are reviewing a probabilistic match pair in the stewardship queue. Both records are from different outpatient clinics in the same health system.

records.record_a: Maria L. Gomez, DOB 1982-04-12, MRN OP-44102, address 118 Oak St
records.record_b: Maria Gomez, DOB 1982-04-12, MRN OP-88719, address 220 Lake Ave
records.conflict: Different phone numbers and addresses; same DOB and similar name

scenarios.question: What is the best stewardship action?
choices: Auto-merge because the score is above 0.90
Reject as not a duplicate because addresses differ
Perform manual review, verify additional evidence per policy, document decision
Create a third duplicate record to preserve both addresses
scenarios.explanation: High scores with demographic conflicts often need manual verification. Coordinators gather evidence, follow policy, and document outcomes.
learningPoints: Scores inform but do not replace judgment
Address changes are common and require context
Documentation supports audit and patient safety

scenarios.title: NICU Name Collision
scenarios.notice: Fictional training scenario for edge-case awareness.
scenarios.context: Two newborns in the NICU have temporary similar names and the same admission date. A probabilistic engine flags a high-similarity pair.

records.record_a: Baby Boy Smith, DOB 2026-03-01, MRN NB-1001
records.context_note: Mother names differ on source records

scenarios.question: What should the coordinator do first?
choices: Merge immediately to prevent duplicate bills
Hold for manual review with NICU registration policy and maternal identifiers
scenarios.explanation: Newborn and twin scenarios are high-risk for false merges. Use policy-driven manual review with additional verifying attributes.
learningPoints: Pediatric and temporary names are high-risk match populations
Threshold changes are governance decisions, not queue shortcuts

interviewQuestions.question: Walk through how you would adjudicate a potential duplicate pair with a high match score but conflicting identifiers.
answerGuide: Confirm the pair context and source systems involved
Check organizational policy for required evidence
Decide merge, reject, or escalate with documentation
followUpQuestions: What evidence would you accept before merging?
When would you escalate to a senior steward or compliance?

interviewQuestions.question: Which metrics would you track to monitor EMPI program health?
answerGuide: Review queue aging and turnaround time
followUpQuestions: How would a rising false-merge rate change your threshold strategy?
